sentences.text: The only known fossil of Tendaguripterus is a single dentary, which serves as the holotype for the species.
This preserved dentary is short, robust, and tall, measuring 25.9 cm in length and reaching a depth of 9.9 cm near its rear.
The jaw becomes over 1.5 times deeper at the back than at the front, creating an extremely deep shape where the teeth project backward rather than upward.
The fragment contains four tooth sockets and two incomplete teeth.
Comparisons with Germanodactylus suggest the wingspan of this animal was about 1 meter wide, while the complete skull length is estimated at 20 cm.
The lower jaw becomes over 1.5 times deeper at the back than at the front, creating an extremely deep shape.
Unlike other dsungaripteroids, the teeth of Tendaguripterus project backward rather than upward or forward.
Based on comparisons with Germanodactylus, the wingspan of Tendaguripterus is estimated to be about 1 meter wide.

German fossil collectors discovered the specimen between 1910 and 1912 at Site Jg during an expedition to the Tendaguru Formation, though material was collected during German expeditions between 1909 and 1913.
Paleontologists David Unwin and Wolf-Dieter Heinrich formally described the fossil as a new genus and species in 1999.
The species was named Tendaguripterus recki in honor of the German geologist Hans Reck.
The genus name combines "Tendaguru", the location of discovery, and the Greek word for wing.
Researchers have proposed that Tendaguripterus was a durophage that fed on hard-shelled invertebrates like bivalves.
Researchers suggest Tendaguripterus likely ate bivalves and other hard-shelled invertebrates.

In 2007, Alexander Kellner and colleagues argued that the resemblance between Tendaguripterus and other dsungaripteroids was superficial and that it might not belong to Pterodactyloidea but rather be a more basal pterosaur.
Kellner and colleagues noted that Tendaguripterus lacks definitive traits of Dsungaripteroidea and cannot be confirmed as a pterodactyloid, so it is placed in the undefined clade Tendaguripteridae.
Kellner and colleagues established the new family Tendaguripteridae to contain Tendaguripterus exclusively, whereas the genus was originally considered a member of the family Germanodactylidae.
Tendaguripterus lived during the Late Kimmeridgian to Early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic period, specifically between 152.21 and 149.2 million years ago during the Kimmeridgian stage.

Tendaguripterus fossils come from the Late Jurassic Tendaguru Formation in southeastern Tanzania, where it lived specifically during the late Kimmeridgian age within the Middle Saurian Member of the formation.

Tendaguripterus lived alongside dinosaurs such as Giraffatitan and Kentrosaurus, as well as other pterosaurs like Rhamphorhynchus and Pterodactylus, in an ecosystem that included shallow marine lagoons, tidal flats, and vegetated inland areas.

It remains unclear whether Tendaguripterus belongs to Dsungaripteroidea or another group, as it has not been included in recent phylogenetic analyses, and Alexander Kellner argued that its resemblance to Germanodactylus and Dsungaripterus was superficial.
